opus-5.5.text:
I don't think of it as a literal goal, like a box we're trying to tick. It's more of a north star, or maybe a useful yardstick. The Erdős problems are a wonderful collection because they span such a wide range. Some are things a strong grad student could knock out in an afternoon if they happened to look at them. Others have resisted the best combinatorialists and number theorists for decades. So the set gives you a gradient of difficulty that's really hard to find elsewhere.

What excites me is less "can the model solve problem number whatever" and more what the attempt tells us about reasoning. When a model makes real progress on an open problem, it can't have memorized the answer, because there isn't one written down anywhere. It has to explore, try ideas, notice when an approach is dead, back up, and stitch together an argument that actually holds. Those are exactly the capabilities we care about well beyond math.

I'd also say we've learned to be humble here. There have been moments where people got excited that a model "solved" an Erdős problem, and it turned out the result was already in the literature somewhere, just obscure. Honestly, that's useful in its own right. A model that can find the forgotten paper that settles a question is valuable to mathematicians. But it's a different thing from new mathematics, and we try to be careful about that distinction.

So if you asked whether we'll eventually solve every Erdős problem, I wouldn't bet against it in the long run. Some of them are probably as hard as anything in mathematics, and some may simply be false or undecidable in interesting ways. The real goal is building systems that mathematicians actually want to work with, ones that are rigorous, honest about what they don't know, and able to push the frontier together with people. If we get that right, the Erdős problems will fall as a side effect.

r001.rationale: The response says that a model’s progress on an open problem can reveal reasoning capabilities, but it does not frame a specific result from the team as evidence of current model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of "solve every Erdős problem" as the goal. It's more like a yardstick that happens to be unusually good.

Erdős left behind something like a thousand problems, and they have a few properties that make them really attractive for us. They're crisp. Each one has a precise statement, so there's no ambiguity about whether you've made progress. They span a huge range of difficulty, from things a strong graduate student could knock out in a weekend to things that have resisted the best people in the field for fifty years. And they're mostly outside the training distribution in the sense that matters, because the open ones don't have solutions written down anywhere. So when a model makes progress, you learn something real about its reasoning rather than its recall.

What we actually care about is whether these systems can do genuine mathematical work: form a plan, try something, notice it's failing, go back, find the right lemma, and produce an argument a human expert can check and build on. The Erdős problems are a dense, honest sample of that kind of work. If the models were just getting good at Erdős problems and nothing else, that would be a sign we'd overfit to the benchmark, and I'd be worried.

So I'd put it this way. If we eventually look up and most of the list is resolved, that would be remarkable, and I wouldn't be shocked over the next several years. But the thing I'd actually be proud of is the model having become a useful collaborator for mathematicians, the kind of thing people reach for on their own open problems. The Erdős list is how we keep ourselves honest on the way there, not the destination.

r001.rationale: The response describes Erdős problems as a yardstick for assessing whether AI systems can do genuine mathematical work, and says model progress on them reveals real reasoning capability.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a compelling long-term goal because it’s concrete, but it spans a huge range of mathematical difficulty. You can make progress on individual problems while still having challenges that are far beyond what current models can do.

For me, the deeper goal would be to build AI that can contribute to mathematics broadly. Solving Erdős problems would be one way to demonstrate that, especially if the models develop ideas and techniques that turn out to be useful elsewhere. I’d care about both which problems we solve and what we learn from solving them.

r001.rationale: The response describes solving Erdős problems as a way to demonstrate broad AI contributions, but does not frame the team’s result as evidence of current model capabilities; it says many challenges remain beyond current models.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s a useful north star. The Erdős problems give us a broad collection of mathematical questions where progress is concrete: can you actually prove something that wasn’t known before? But I wouldn’t want to confuse solving that collection with solving mathematics. The deeper goal is to build models that can help mathematicians discover things, develop useful ideas, and understand why a result is true. Solving every Erdős problem would be an extraordinary milestone along that path.
